items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

On October 9, 2026, around 17:55–18:06 UTC, opening Codex cloud sessions in the Android ChatGPT/Codex interface and mobile web showed “Sesión no encontrada” (“Session not found”). I have encountered this with all sessions I have tried.

This prevents me from opening the sessions, continuing work, or reliably checking and stopping a potentially active task.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The observed sequence on the affected account is:

1. Open an existing Codex cloud session in the Android app.
2. See “Sesión no encontrada” instead of the session.
3. Try opening the session through mobile web.
4. Encounter the same access problem.
5. Repeat with another existing cloud session.

The original trigger is unknown; this is an account-specific observation, not a confirmed reproduction on a clean account.

### What is the expected behavior?

Existing cloud sessions should open with their history and current state. I should be able to continue or stop an active task, or receive an actionable recovery message. Recovery should preserve the history and existing work.

### Additional information

- Android version, app version, browser/version, and web build: not captured.
- During troubleshooting, dot could retrieve history and status for two affected sessions. The older one reported `inProgress` with `error: null`; the newer one had completed and was waiting for instructions.
- Sending follow-up instructions through dot to those exact, user-verified session IDs returned `CloudThreadNotFoundError` / `NOT_FOUND`.
- Showing the task card again did not restore access.
- The readable history is not evidence that the older task is still executing, and we could not confirm that it had stopped. No data deletion has been established.
- The mobile UI error and dot's follow-up error may come from different paths; a shared cause has not been established.

Related reports: #50136 and #50168 cover cross-client visibility and readable cloud tasks whose follow-up submission returns NOT_FOUND. This report adds the inability to open affected sessions on both Android and mobile web.

Prepared with AI assistance at my request. Account details, session/environment identifiers, repository names, private content, and screenshots are omitted.

items.body:
## Windows sandbox setup refresh failure blocks all local tools

A Windows Codex Desktop installation repeatedly fails before any local command starts:

`Failed to create unified exec process: helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors`

The same failure occurs for simple read-only commands such as `Get-Location`, and `node_repl` exits during startup. The project code is not involved; the failure happens during Codex Windows sandbox initialization.

### Environment

- Windows 11 x64, build 26300
- Codex Desktop AppX package: 26.1002.7124.0
- Codex doctor runtime: 26.1002.52244, build 13536
- Installed through the Windows/Codex desktop app
- `%USERPROFILE%\\.codex\\config.toml` initially contained:

```toml
[windows]
sandbox = "elevated"
```

### Observed diagnostics

- `CodexSandboxService.OpenAI.Codex` was installed but stopped.
- `HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\OpenAI\\Codex\\WindowsSandboxService\\RegisteredCore` was missing.
- Normal Codex tool startup failed with `helper_unknown_error: setup refresh had errors`.
- Running the same command through an explicitly elevated terminal succeeded, showing the project and shell were healthy.

### Control / workaround

Changing only the Codex user configuration to:

```toml
[windows]
sandbox = "unelevated"
```

made `codex sandbox -- whoami` succeed. The normal desktop tool channel requires a full Codex restart to pick up the setting.

This workaround weakens the elevated sandbox isolation and is not a satisfactory permanent fix. Another user on the same day reported the same problem, suggesting a broader regression rather than a project-specific issue.

Please investigate the Windows sandbox setup/refresh path, especially Registered Core provisioning, the stopped service, and the elevated setup failure. Please provide a supported fix that preserves existing projects, chats, and configuration. Related reports: #52482 and #52601.

items.title: Prevent brokered credential aliases from bypassing MITM hooks
items.body:
Prevent brokered credential aliases from bypassing MITM hooks

## Why

A credential bound to a host with MITM hooks could also be used at an alias without hooks, allowing the proxy to inject the real credential without enforcing hook policy.

## What changed

Reject requests to unhooked aliases when their selected brokered credentials are also bound to a hooked host. Check both HTTP forwarding and MITM requests before replacing dummy credentials, returning `403` with `blocked-by-mitm-hook` for denied requests.

Use the same destination and credential-selection rules for alias checks and injection, including configured URL prefixes, safe paths, equivalent credentials, merged Basic authentication fields, and environment scope.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for built-in and configured provider aliases, IPv6 destinations, credential selection, and unrelated credentials. Add an agent-started proxy test that verifies credential masking and alias denial.

items.title: Handle completion events in either order in shell snapshot tests
items.body:
Handle completion events in either order in shell snapshot tests

## Why

A tool can return before its background watcher emits `ExecCommandEnd`. Waiting for that event first can discard an earlier `TurnComplete`, causing the shell snapshot test helper to time out.

## What changed

Update `run_tool_turn_on_harness` to track both the matching `ExecCommandEnd` and `TurnComplete` in a single event loop, returning only after both have arrived regardless of order.

items.title: Add an opt-in feature for subagent model context defaults
items.body:
Add an opt-in feature for subagent model context defaults

## What changed

Add the disabled-by-default `subagent_default_context_limits` feature and expose it in the configuration schema. When enabled, shared configuration for spawning and resuming subagents clears inherited `model_context_window` and `model_auto_compact_token_limit` overrides so subagents use their model's default context window and auto-compaction threshold.

items.title: Linux sandbox 0.162: deny_read entries that name the same file through a symlink fail with "Unable to mount source on destination: No such file or directory"

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
Follow-up to #43929. Thanks for the fix in #50059, which works. With it in place, a second failure now shows.

**Setup:** Linux x86_64, Fedora Atomic (Bazzite), where `/home` is a symlink to `/var/home`. A managed `requirements.toml` denies single files under both spellings, so the deny holds whichever path a command uses:

```toml
deny_read = ["/var/home/user/.codex/auth.json", "/home/user/.codex/auth.json"]
```

**Result on 0.162.0 (desktop 26.1007.21434, bundled engine 0.162.0-alpha.17.2):** `codex sandbox -- /usr/bin/true` fails with both system bubblewrap 0.12.0 and Codex's bundled bubblewrap:

```
bwrap: Can't bind mount /bindfileXXXXXX on /newroot/var/home/user/.codex/auth.json: Unable to mount source on destination: No such file or directory
```

0.156.1 with the same policy works when given a bwrap without the #43929 descriptor bug.

**Cause:** the bwrap argument list now holds two masks for one file:

```
--ro-bind-data 3 /home/user/.codex/auth.json
...
--ro-bind-data 6 /var/home/user/.codex/auth.json
```

bubblewrap removes each bind-data temp file right after mounting it. The second mount therefore targets a deleted file, and the kernel returns ENOENT. Minimal repro without Codex:

```sh
d=$(mktemp -d); mkdir $d/real; echo x > $d/real/f; ln -s real $d/alias
bwrap --ro-bind / / --dev /dev --ro-bind-data 3 $d/alias/f --ro-bind-data 4 $d/real/f -- true 3</dev/null 4</dev/null
# Unable to mount source on destination: No such file or directory
```

The same happens when one path is simply listed twice. 0.156 built masks from `get_unreadable_roots_with_cwd`; 0.162 uses `get_unreadable_roots_with_cwd_preserving_symlinks`, so aliases are no longer merged, possibly since #48155.

**Suggested fix:** before adding single-file masks, drop any file mask whose resolved target was already masked. Directory masks (`--tmpfs`) are not affected.

## Summary

During a previously working, long-running coding session in Codex Desktop, normal GPT-6.1 Sol requests suddenly began failing with HTTP 503 and a **Daybreak Blue access verification** error. **Usage quota was still available when the first 503 occurred.** This was an ordinary coding workflow; I had not enabled or requested Daybreak Blue access.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- Client: Codex Desktop
- Subscription: ChatGPT Plus
- Model: GPT-6.1 Sol
- Authentication: Sign in with ChatGPT

## Exact error

```text
unexpected status 503 Service Unavailable: {"detail":"Unable to verify Daybreak Blue access. Please try again."}, url: https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses, cf-ray: a47ee4d2fb4ac0ba-LAX, request id: ba1c1a64-7c7a-4d74-a58a-2e7e2c0f7bb1
```

- HTTP status: **503 Service Unavailable**
- Endpoint: `https://chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses`
- Request ID: `ba1c1a64-7c7a-4d74-a58a-2e7e2c0f7bb1`
- Cloudflare Ray: `a47ee4d2fb4ac0ba-LAX`

## Timeline / steps to reproduce (observed)

1. Use Codex Desktop normally with GPT-6.1 Sol in an existing coding project/session.
2. After previously successful work, request another continuation during the ongoing session.
3. The request fails with the above 503 error; retries may also fail.
4. **Important: the first failure happened before the user's usage quota was exhausted.** The quota became exhausted later, and must not be treated as the initial cause.

## Expected behavior

Normal Codex requests should continue when the user has quota, or return an accurate, actionable error if a service is temporarily unavailable.

## Actual behavior

A standard coding request receives `Unable to verify Daybreak Blue access` even though no Daybreak Blue feature was intentionally enabled or used.

## Investigation request

Please trace the request ID to identify which access/entitlement check returned 503 and why it affected a normal GPT-6.1 Sol coding session. It is not yet established whether this is an entitlement-service outage, routing/state inconsistency, or another backend issue.

## Prior report

Re-submitted after the GitHub profile was renamed. Earlier report: #52650 (closed at the user's request; same issue).

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop app on Linux (Bazzite 44, KDE Plasma 6.7.5, Wayland), with a local MCP stdio plugin.

### What feature would you like to see?

First-party Linux desktop control through public XDG RemoteDesktop/ScreenCast portals: screenshots, pointer input, scrolling and keyboard input, with local OS consent, visible emergency stop, clear session lifecycle and optional KDE-approved remembered permission.

I built an experimental MIT-licensed prototype with Codex and am sharing it for engineering review:
https://github.com/quantumbitdynamics-collab/linux-desktop-control

The repository contains the implementation, setup instructions, 27 automated tests, dependency/license notices and an explicit REVIEW_STATUS.txt. It does not include desktop screenshots, transcripts, permission tokens or personal configuration. It uses portal-authorized PipeWire streams and public D-Bus methods, without root, /dev/uinput, private KWin input APIs or a publicly exposed control endpoint.

### Additional information

Live tests verified MCP discovery, screenshot capture, clicks, scrolling, keyboard input, stop and disconnect on one KDE/Wayland display. A spoken request delegated into an existing Codex task completed a harmless button/text/scroll/capture/stop demo. Continuous sessions worked; KDE returned a remembered-permission token. Prompt-free token reuse has NOT yet been verified.

This is a proof of concept, not production-ready. Follow-up interactive tests exposed high speech-to-action latency, repetitive acknowledgements, keyboard modifier/case inconsistencies, an unintended multi-selection, and focus/animation races. Function-key chords such as Alt+F4 are not currently supported by the prototype's key allowlist. Other desktops, X11, multi-monitor/scaling, direct native voice-tool invocation and ChatGPT web/mobile integration remain unverified.

I would welcome guidance on whether this approach could inform first-party Linux computer-use support, or where a community implementation should be contributed. This is related to #20851, but specifically proposes a Linux portal backend and shares a runnable prototype rather than requesting a macOS CLI entry point. I understand review or adoption is not guaranteed.

items.title: Bound local exec-server output draining after process exit
items.body:
Bound local exec-server output draining after process exit

## Why

A local command can exit while a descendant keeps its inherited output pipes open, delaying `exec_command` completion and turn completion.

## What changed

Start the bounded output drain when a local exec-server process exits, whether exit is reported by an event or recovered through `process/read`. Remote execution continues waiting for output closure so buffered or delayed output is retained.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for local shell snapshot execution completing before a descendant releases stdout, preserving the foreground output and exit code. Add remote event-stream cases that retain output arriving after both reported and recovered process exit.

items.title: Linux sandbox panics when a permission profile grants write access to individual files

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
### Codex version

`codex-cli 0.162.0`

### Platform

- Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux x86_64)
- bubblewrap 0.9.0

### Description

A custom permission profile that grants write access to individual files causes the Linux sandbox helper to panic. The sandbox treats each writable regular file as though it were a directory and appends synthetic credential-directory paths such as `.aws`.

The documented permission-profile format allows a workspace to be broadly readable while narrower descendants are writable, but an exact writable file produces a filesystem panic instead of being enforced or rejected cleanly.

### Minimal permission profile

```toml
[permissions.knife-docs]
description = "Read the repository; edit selected planning documents."

[permissions.knife-docs.filesystem]
":minimal" = "read"

[permissions.knife-docs.filesystem."/home/brian/RustroverProjects/knife-sharpening-trainer"]
"." = "read"
"AGENTS.md" = "write"
"README.md" = "write"
"docs/roadmap.md" = "write"
"hardware/prototype-v1.md" = "write"
```

The selected profile file contains:

```toml
default_permissions = "knife-docs"
approval_policy = "on-request"
```

### Reproduction

```bash
codex sandbox -p knife-docs -P knife-docs \
  -C /home/brian/RustroverProjects/knife-sharpening-trainer \
  /usr/bin/true
```

The same panic occurs while bootstrapping a fresh interactive TUI session with `codex --profile knife-docs -C ...`.

### Actual result

```text
bwrap: loopback: Failed RTM_NEWADDR: Operation not permitted

thread 'main' panicked at linux-sandbox/src/linux_run_main.rs:1275:21:
failed to inspect synthetic bubblewrap mount target /home/brian/RustroverProjects/knife-sharpening-trainer/hardware/prototype-v1.md/.aws: Not a directory (os error 20)
```

There is also a host-level user-namespace restriction producing the bubblewrap loopback failure. However, selecting the built-in `:read-only` profile produces only that bubblewrap error. Adding exact-file write rules introduces the additional Rust panic and invalid `FILE/.aws` mount target.

Replacing the exact-file write rules with directory-level write rules avoids the `FILE/.aws` panic.

### Expected result

Codex should enforce exact-file write permissions as documented. If the active Linux sandbox cannot enforce them, it should return a clear configuration/runtime error and must not panic or construct child paths beneath a regular file.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed workflow:

1. Open a browser-based 3D application in the Codex desktop app's built-in browser, associated with a managed cloud project.
2. Enter annotation mode and add several comments on the rendered page.
3. Attempt to send the annotations together to the agent.
4. Observe “Error submitting message” with the decoded-message-length error above.

The exact annotation count, selected areas, viewport dimensions, image sizes, and minimum triggering batch size have not yet been captured. A private application was involved; no private URL, settings, conversation identifiers, or original screenshot are published here.

Ordinary text messages and a separately attached screenshot of the error successfully reached the agent afterward.

### What is the expected behavior?

Users should be able to submit an ordinary batch of browser annotations. The annotation workflow should fit the limits of its actual message transport, using separate attachment uploads, appropriate image resizing/compression, or safe chunking where necessary.

If submission cannot fit, provide a preflight warning and a way to split/retry the batch while preserving all annotations and comments.

### Additional information

The error establishes a decoded message size limit, but does not establish which component, transport, or payload field exceeds it. Embedded annotation screenshots/context are a possible investigation lead, not a confirmed cause. No client-side source or rejected payload was inspected.

Potential workarounds to test: send smaller annotation batches, or use a cropped screenshot with a numbered text list. These have not been verified as fixes for this specific failure.

Duplicate searches for the exact error, byte count, and annotation/4-MiB combinations did not find the same report. Related but distinct: #52156 reports a 64-MiB decoded-message limit in a long-running cloud thread, without the annotation trigger described here. A shared root cause is not established.

Reported on October 9, 2026; the exact failure timestamp is unavailable. This issue is submitted at the affected user's explicit request, following the official desktop troubleshooting documentation's GitHub reporting route.

items.title: Limit daemon feature compatibility checks to explicit CLI overrides
items.body:
Limit daemon feature compatibility checks to explicit CLI overrides

## Why

A running shared background server owns its feature settings until it restarts. Differences from a client's configuration files or defaults should not trigger a compatibility warning or a restart request.

## What changed

- Check shared-service features only when explicitly overridden on the command line.
- Exclude overrides superseded by active legacy managed configuration or feature requirements, while supporting older servers without `configRequirements/read`.
- Pass only the remaining explicit feature overrides to a requested daemon restart.

## Testing

Update compatibility tests for stale daemon overrides, explicit enable/disable requests, managed configuration, and older servers. Extend CLI startup tests to verify the feature overrides persisted after a restart.

labels.name: bug

items.body:
## Summary
On Windows 10 Home x64 (10.0.19045), Codex CLI 0.162.0 communicates with the model in a TUI session, but a trivial shell command does not return observable output or an exit status.

The supplied TUI trace reaches `unified_exec.open_session` and `codex.process.spawn`. Approximately 31 seconds later, the outer code-mode operation yields `Script running with cell ID 1` with empty output. No matching final child-process result is visible before shutdown. This is **not** a confirmed ConPTY deadlock or a completely frozen TUI.

## Environment
- Codex CLI 0.162.0, npm, windows-x86_64
- Windows 10 Home x64, build 19045; UBR unknown
- Preferred shell CMD; actual console host/version unverified
- Model gpt-6.1-sol; ChatGPT authentication
- Current sandbox `unelevated` per user; earlier doctor recorded `elevated` provisioning failure (`helper_unknown_error`)
- TUI trace policy WorkspaceWrite, network false, approvals Never
- Effective flags in captured turn: `unified_exec=true`, `code_mode_host=true`, `shell_snapshot=true`
- `terminal.type=unknown` is telemetry metadata, not proof of a ConPTY fault

## Reproduction observed
1. Start Codex CLI 0.162.0 TUI on affected Windows machine.
2. Ask it to run `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /d /c echo CODEX_TUI_TEST`.
3. The model calls `tools.exec_command` via code-mode, without explicitly specifying shell/login/tty.
4. The call is approved and enters `codex.process.spawn`, but no final stdout or child exit code appears.

## Sanitized trace (2026-10-09 UTC)
```text
16:52:09.977  model response.completed
16:52:10.039  exec_command received via code_mode
16:52:10.052  unified_exec.exec_command mode=resumable
16:52:10.052  unified_exec.open_session: new
16:52:10.053  tool_decision: approved (Config)
16:52:10.077  codex.process.spawn: codex_sandboxing::spawn: new
16:52:41.043  outer code-mode result:
              Script running with cell ID 1
              Wall time 31.0 seconds
              Output: [empty]
16:52:44.028  subsequent model response.completed
16:53:08      session shutdown begins
```
The outer `success=true` concerns the code-mode envelope, **not** the child exit status. `outcome=interrupted` appears, but its precise cause is unknown. There is no follow-up wait in the supplied trace.

Earlier `codex doctor` (15:53:55 UTC) reported `sandbox backend=elevated`, `sandbox provisioning=failed`, `error code=helper_unknown_error`. The earlier diagnostic and later TUI symptom are not proven causally related. Doctor stdout was redirected, so its terminal handles do not establish those of the later TUI.

## Comparisons
User-reported `codex exec` with permanent `unelevated` configuration returned `CODEX_PERMANENT_OK` and exit code 0. Exact successful noninteractive tool trace is unavailable, so equivalent child-process execution is not independently verified.

User-reported interactive tests with `--no-daemon`, `--disable code_mode_host`, and `--disable shell_snapshot` did not resolve the symptom. The captured trace has the latter two features enabled and does not independently document the disabled-feature runs.

The sandbox.log and current config.toml were unavailable to the reviewer. No actual console host identification, ConPTY error, Windows error 32/1385, or Defender block was established.

## Related issues
- #32855 — elevated helper_unknown_error with unelevated working
- #52179 — desktop runtime ACL/file-lock issue; no such error established here
- #52434 — generic Windows sandbox setup error
These may be related but no duplicate is established. The private desktop opt-out was removed in #46554; it has not been used as a workaround.

## Maintainer questions
1. How can we distinguish waiting in the Windows sandbox wrapper, child shell creation, or resumable exec transport at `codex.process.spawn`?
2. Is a one-invocation read-only A/B test with `--disable unified_exec` supported on CLI 0.162.0?
3. Which sanitized traces should be collected to correlate the earlier elevated provisioning error with this later TUI hang?
4. Is there a known fix for this specific Windows 10 CLI path?

No Windows security settings, ACLs, project files, configuration, histories, or databases were reset during the documentary review. Raw logs, account identifiers, tokens, and private paths are intentionally excluded.

items.title: Windows: headless codex exec inherits the desktop app's computer-use runtime (MCP + notify hook); idle helper respawns; machine unusable under parallel load

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: exec
labels.description: Issues related to the `codex exec` subcommand

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?
codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.2 (the codex.exe shipped with the Codex desktop app OpenAI.Codex 26.1002.7124.0, Microsoft Store package)

### What subscription do you have?
ChatGPT Pro

### Which model were you using?
gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort high), headless `codex exec`

### What platform is your computer?
Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200 (x64), AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 95 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 5070 12 GB

### What terminal emulator and version are you using?
None: headless `codex exec` launched from a PowerShell 7 queue runner (stdin prompt, -o output file)

### What issue are you seeing?
## 1. Summary (please read this first)

We run Codex heavily on one Windows workstation: on 9 Oct about 19 headless `codex exec` runs started by our own queue script, in parallel, plus the desktop app. That is our own choice of workload and we are not claiming the CLI should handle unlimited parallelism.

What we can show with measurements:

1. **Every headless `codex exec` run starts the desktop app's computer-use runtime.** The desktop app writes an MCP server (`node_repl.exe` from its `cua_node` runtime), a `notify` hook (`codex-computer-use.exe turn-ended`) and the `unified-computer-use` plugin into the shared `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml`. Headless runs read the same file, so each one spawns `node_repl.exe`, `codex-code-mode-host.exe` and `node ./mcp/server.mjs`, and fires the computer-use notifier at every turn end. With ~20 runs that is roughly 40–60 extra long-lived processes (we counted 20 `node_repl.exe` and 18 `codex-code-mode-host.exe` at 17:21 on 9 Oct) that our runs never use.
2. **The desktop app keeps an idle computer-use helper alive for many hours** (`codex-computer-use-swift.exe` running from 8 Oct 19:46 until we killed it on 9 Oct 15:39, with no computer-use work in between) and restarts it immediately when it is killed.
3. **The GPU memory that Windows attributes to `dwm.exe` grows almost every day** (about 0.3 GB/h on average, in bursts) and only a dwm restart or a reboot brings it back down. We have had to restart dwm on 4, 5, 6 (twice) and 9 (twice) Oct, and force a reboot on 2 Oct.

What we **cannot** show, and do not claim:

- We hoped to prove that the dwm memory is released when the Codex processes exit. **Our own measurement on 9 Oct does not support that.** Right after we killed all Codex processes (17:33:21–17:33:38), dwm's dedicated GPU memory was still 4,416 MB. It dropped to 658 MB only after we restarted dwm at 17:34:00. See section 4.
- An hourly correlation between dwm growth and the number of Codex/computer-use processes over 8–9 Oct was essentially zero (Pearson r = −0.08, n = 40 hours). An earlier analysis (2–4 Oct) found growth only while computer-use sessions were open. The evidence on dwm is mixed.

We are therefore reporting (1) and (2) as concrete defects, and (3) as a recurring problem we would like you to help investigate with the reproduction script in Appendix A.

## 2. Environment

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| OS | Windows 11 Home, 10.0.26200 |
| CPU / RAM | AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (16 cores / 32 threads), 95 GB RAM |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 12 GB (driver 32.0.16.1062) + AMD Radeon integrated graphics |
| Codex CLI | `codex-cli 0.162.0-alpha.2` (binary under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\…\codex.exe`) |
| Codex app | `OpenAI.Codex 26.1002.7124.0` (`ChatGPT.exe`) |
| Headless invocation | `codex exec --skip-git-repo-check -C <dir> -m gpt-6.1-sol -c model_reasoning_effort="high" -s danger-full-access -o <file> -` (prompt on stdin), one process per job, launched by a PowerShell queue runner |
| Typical parallelism | 3–20 headless runs; some runs start Playwright/headless Chrome for page QA |
| Metric | Windows performance counter `\GPU Process Memory(*)\Dedicated Usage`, summed for the dwm.exe PID, sampled every 2 minutes |

Note on the metric: this counter can exceed the physical VRAM (we have seen 54 GB against a 12 GB card), so it counts shared/aliased allocations, not physical VRAM. We use it because its growth tracks the user-visible lag on several days, not because it is a precise VRAM figure.

## 3. Defects we can reproduce from configuration alone

### 3.1 Headless `codex exec` starts the desktop computer-use runtime

Observed in `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\config.toml` (written by the desktop app; values shown without secrets):

```toml
notify = [ "%LOCALAPPDATA%\\OpenAI\\Codex\\runtimes\\cua_node\\<hash>\\bin\\node_modules\\@oai\\sky\\bin\\windows\\codex-computer-use.exe", "turn-ended" ]
[plugins."unified-computer-use@openai-bundled"]
[mcp_servers.node_repl]
command = '%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\runtimes\cua_node\<hash>\bin\node_repl.exe'
```

Observed result: when our queue runner killed one headless run's process tree on 9 Oct, the tree contained `codex.exe exec …`, `node_repl.exe` (cua_node runtime), `codex-code-mode-host.exe` and `node.exe ./mcp/server.mjs`, all children of the headless run. At 17:21 the machine had 22 `codex.exe`, 18 `codex-code-mode-host.exe` and 20 `node_repl.exe`.

Expected: a headless, non-interactive `codex exec` should not start the desktop app's computer-use / browser-control runtime or its turn-ended notifier unless the run asks for it. At minimum, there should be a documented way (flag or profile) to run `exec` without the app-installed MCP servers and notify hook, and the app should not silently make them global for the CLI.

### 3.2 Idle computer-use helper is kept alive and respawned

Observed: `codex-computer-use-swift.exe` (parent `ChatGPT.exe`) had been running since 8 Oct 19:46 with no computer-use work; a `node server.mjs` and a `node_repl.exe` from the same runtime had been running since 9 Oct 00:39. We killed them at 15:39:48–15:39:53; the app started the helper again at 15:39:48.

Expected: the helper exits when no computer-use session is active, or at least after an idle timeout.

### 3.3 Orphaned children after a timed-out tool call (reported internally, not re-measured today)

When a shell tool call inside `codex exec` timed out, its children (python, node, a headless browser, ripgrep) survived and inherited the run's stdout pipe. The pipe never closed, so our runner and its queue slot stayed blocked for hours. We worked around it on 8 Oct by putting each run in a Windows job object and killing the job's tree. Expected: Codex terminates the whole process tree of a timed-out tool call on Windows.

### 3.4 Antivirus load from Codex session files (observation)

A 2-minute Microsoft Defender performance recording on 9 Oct showed the session rollout files under `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\sessions` being scanned 30–50 times each, and `codex.exe` triggering 29 process-start scans (8.6 s). Defender had read ~7 TB in 65 hours on this machine; Codex was one of several contributors. Adding an exclusion for the sessions folder reduced Defender's read rate (278 → ~83 MB/s, together with other exclusions). A note in the Windows docs about this, or fewer rewrites of the rollout files, would help.

## 4. The 9 Oct incident, with timestamps

| Time | dwm dedicated GPU memory | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 00:00 → 15:36 | 18,777 → 23,453 MB | Steady growth in bursts, ~0.30 GB/h |
| 15:37 | 23,453 → 1,493 MB | dwm restarted (UAC). User had reported lag. |
| 15:39 | 1,73x MB | Idle computer-use helper and its node processes killed (3.2) |
| 16:20–16:24 | 3,041 → 4,322 MB | +1.3 GB in 4 minutes, then flat at 4.2–4.5 GB |
| 17:09–17:31 | 4,347–4,464 MB | 80–182 Playwright/Chrome processes, 12–20 cua `node_repl` processes, 887–1,018 top-level windows |
| 17:21 | 4,404 MB | Machine unusable: a few frames per second, cursor flicker, busy spinner; system drive ~92 % busy |
| 17:33:18–17:33:38 | — | All 21 `codex.exe` killed (18 from our queue runner, 2 from the desktop app, 1 whose parent had already exited) plus their children |
| **17:33:38** | **4,416 MB** | **After the kill, before any dwm restart** |
| 17:34:00 | — | dwm restarted (new PID) |
| 17:34:17 | 658 MB | First sample of the new dwm process |
| 17:36:12 | 1,538 MB | New dwm process settles at its usual starting level |

Our honest reading: on 9 Oct the user-visible lag at 17:21 was most likely caused by total machine load (about 20 parallel runs, their helper processes, up to 182 browser processes and a saturated system drive), not by dwm's 4.4 GB. Killing Codex did not reduce dwm's memory; restarting dwm did.

## 5. Recurrence and impact

| Date | Symptom | dwm counter | Recovery | Codex involvement (our assessment) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Oct 07:31–07:55 | Freeze ~21 min, ~1 fps, black screens | ~11.6 GB | Resolved on its own before the computer-use helper was closed | Unclear |
| 2 Oct 10:47–11:13 | Freeze 26 min | 52.9–54.4 GB | Forced reboot; terminal output of the crashed session was lost | ~29 computer-use sessions were closed at 10:57–11:01 without recovery |
| 2 Oct evening | Lag | 3.5 → 26.8 GB in 9 h | None that day; the counter kept growing to 42 GB on 3 Oct | Possible, not proven |
| 3–4 Oct | Lag, alarm above 30 GB | 29.9 → 43.7 GB | dwm restart 4 Oct 21:27 (43.1 → 1.5 GB) | Growth 0.9–3.7 GB/h only while computer-use sessions were open; flat for 31 h without them (estimate, no controlled test) |
| 5 Oct 16:00 | Lag | 8.2 GB | dwm restart; main load was elsewhere (file-explorer windows) | Not the main cause |
| 6 Oct | Lag, twice | 18.9–33.1 GB | dwm restarts 05:13 and 18:34; reboot 23:03 | CPU saturation, Codex one of several loads |
| 7–8 Oct | No lag reported | 4.3 → 18.6 GB | — | — |
| 9 Oct | Lag, twice | 22.9 GB; 4.4 GB | dwm restarts 15:37 and 17:34; all headless runs killed | See section 4 |

Impact on work: every episode stops the operator (the machine is not usable for dictation or review), and each one has taken 10–30 minutes to diagnose and recover; on 2 Oct it took a forced reboot and lost a session's output; on 9 Oct the evening's queued Codex work had to be killed and restarted. Not every incident above is caused by Codex; we list them all so you can see the full pattern.


### Update, 9 Oct evening
- With at most 3 parallel headless runs (we capped our queue after the incident), dwm's counter grew from 0.65 GB (after the 17:34 restart) to about 2.0 GB and then stayed flat for 1.5 h (1.99 GB at 17:56, 2.07 GB at 18:22, 2.00 GB at 19:15).
- `%USERPROFILE%\.codex\thread_history_1.sqlite` on this machine is 16.7 GB (created 22 Sep, still written on 9 Oct). Is this expected, and is it safe to compact or prune?

### What is the expected behavior?
## 6. What we are asking for

1. **Fix 3.1:** headless `codex exec` should not inherit the desktop app's computer-use MCP server, plugin and notify hook by default, or there should be a supported switch to disable them for `exec`.
2. **Fix 3.2:** the computer-use helper should exit when idle.
3. **Fix 3.3:** terminate the whole process tree of a timed-out tool call on Windows.
4. **Investigate the dwm growth** with the script in Appendix A (we will run it ourselves and share the CSV if useful). Specifically: does the computer-use runtime or the `notify` hook create graphics-capture or DirectComposition resources even in headless runs?


### Additional information
## Appendix A. Reproduction experiment (not yet run)

Script: available on request (PowerShell, samples dwm GPU memory and process counts every minute). It never restarts dwm.

- **Phase A, baseline:** 10 minutes, no Codex runs.
- **Phase B, load:** start N headless `codex exec` runs (default 10) whose prompt only runs a long `Start-Sleep`, so the runs do no UI or browser work; sample for 30 minutes.
- **Phase C, after close:** kill only the process trees the script started; sample for 15 minutes.
- **Every minute:** dwm dedicated and shared GPU memory (MB), dwm PID, counts of `codex.exe`, `node_repl.exe`, `codex-code-mode-host.exe`, `chrome.exe`, and visible top-level windows → CSV.
- **Run it twice:** once with the app-written `config.toml` (computer-use MCP server and notify hook present) and once with a clean `CODEX_HOME` (no MCP servers, no notify). That separates the CLI itself from the inherited desktop runtime.
- **Reading the result:** growth in B and a drop in C with the same dwm PID means Codex processes hold the memory. Growth in B with no drop in C means dwm retains it, and only a dwm restart helps (what we saw on 9 Oct). No growth in B means headless Codex alone does not reproduce it.

## Appendix B. Limits of this report

- The dwm counter is not physical VRAM (see section 2).
- Measurements come from our own monitoring scripts at 2-minute intervals; the 17:21 frame-rate and disk-busy figures are the operator's observation and a one-off measurement, not logged series.
- Our workload includes many non-Codex processes (Playwright browsers, a Claude desktop session, screenshot tools, file-explorer windows). We have not isolated Codex in a controlled test yet; Appendix A is that test.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

App (macOS desktop)

### What feature would you like to see?

Please make each subagent's model, provider, and reasoning effort consistently visible in the agent list, child detail panel, and relevant failure diagnostics, across both V1 and V2.

The parent chat's selected model does not establish which model each child used. An agent name, role, status, and result summary are insufficient to audit a run that uses different models or providers.

A compact label could look like:

`site_design · GPT-6.1 Sol · high`

The detail view should show the configured provider/model and, where available, the resolved route or server-reported serving identity. These are different evidence levels: if the backend does not report the actual serving model, please say so rather than presenting a requested selector as verified serving identity.

#### Concrete observed workflow

In a local desktop implementation task investigated on October 8, 2026:

1. The parent ran on `anthropic/claude-fable-5-1` through a custom OpenCodex provider.
2. The parent explicitly spawned two V2 children, `site_design` and `pipeline`, requesting `gpt-6.1-sol` with `high` reasoning effort.
3. The child session records confirmed those configured model/effort values; proxy request logs showed the children routed to the native OpenAI backend.
4. A child sent an encrypted V2 message back to the Claude parent. The next parent request was rejected with `unreadable_encrypted_agent_task`.
5. The main model had not changed when the first failure occurred. The missing child configuration in the user-facing agent view made the failure initially look like an unexplained encryption error in an unchanged Claude conversation.

The model and routing information had to be recovered from child records and proxy logs. It should be visible in the App when supervising the agents.

This example motivates the visibility request. The quoted error comes from the third-party proxy; this report does not ask the App team to fix that proxy or claim the App ignored a model override.

#### Requested behavior

- Show each child's configured model/provider and reasoning effort next to its name, with details available without inspecting local storage.
- Distinguish explicit overrides, role configuration, inheritance, and any observable routing fallback or model change.
- Label resolved routing and server-reported serving identity accurately; render unavailable values as unknown.
- Preserve the information for active, completed, failed, and resumed children.
- In errors involving a child or child-to-parent message, identify the relevant agent and its configuration where known, so the user can see which model/provider boundary is involved.
- Use the same supported child metadata for live and replayed UI views.

V1 is currently used in this setup to avoid the encrypted V2 handoff problem. Model visibility should remain consistent when switching collaboration surfaces.

### Additional information

Current installed desktop app: `26.1002.52244` (build `13536`, read from the installed app's bundle metadata).
Platform: macOS, `Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`.
The investigated child runs recorded bundled Codex CLI `0.162.0-alpha.2`.

Related open issues found before filing:

- #32283 — Subagents panel omits model and reasoning effort.
- #39542 — Effective provider/model/effort/service-tier visibility for V2 subagents.
- #51377 — Model/effort visibility differs between assistant-created and manually created tasks.
- #17312 — Effective provider/model display can diverge from the child configuration.
- #32504 — Missing effective child metadata in canonical V2 activity items.
- #47779 — Persist the server-reported served model, separately from the requested model.

This report adds the concrete child-to-parent failure-diagnosis case and asks for consistent visibility across V1/V2 and failed/resumed runs. It overlaps the requests above and is linked here so maintainers can consolidate it with the appropriate existing work.

I'm a ChatGPT Pro subscriber using Codex GPT-6.1 Sol with Ultra reasoning and Fast mode enabled for a substantial Rust, Flutter, and Yocto engineering project.

The agent received an unusually complete engineering handoff: independently audited findings, a corrected 219-package implementation queue, reproduction tests, candidate fixes, regression criteria, and clean Git worktrees.

Performance concerns

Despite Ultra + Fast, progress was unexpectedly slow. After approximately four hours, only two implementation PRs had been opened. The agent later acknowledged spending excessive time coordinating, personally implementing routine fixes, repeating full test suites, and performing unnecessary analysis.

Subagent utilization appeared far below expectations for this workload.

Implementation-quality concerns

Codex repeatedly reported extensive passing tests and independent reviews. However, GitHub's automated Codex reviews subsequently identified nine potential defects across PRs #40 and #41, including four P1 findings.

An attempted deployment to our development hardware also caused Socket integrations to disappear. The system was recovered, but the deployment tooling required substantial additional correction.

Impact

I spent several hours supervising and correcting the agent instead of making the expected engineering progress. I ultimately decided to transfer implementation back to another coding system.

Request

Please escalate this for investigation into GPT-6.1 Sol Ultra + Fast performance, subagent coordination efficiency, and implementation quality.

I'd appreciate clarification on whether this behavior is expected, whether there are known performance regressions, and whether there is a recommended configuration for large, multi-agent engineering workloads.

items.title: [TUI] “This server is not managed by Codex” obscures daemon ownership and safe recovery

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: TUI
labels.description: Issues related to the terminal user interface: text input, menus and dialogs, and terminal display

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Summary

When the TUI finds a reachable shared app-server with incompatible feature flags, it can disable **Restart with these settings** with:

```text
This server is not managed by Codex.
```

This message is misleading. The condition checked is whether the **Codex app-server daemon manager recognizes the running backend**, not whether the server was launched by a Codex client. Codex Desktop/CLI can launch an app-server that is not owned by that particular daemon manager. The message sounds like the user has started an external server and does not explain what prevents a restart or how to recover safely.

This issue focuses on the **TUI diagnostic and recovery choices**. It does not propose adopting or force-restarting a process without established ownership.

## Observed behavior

In the shared-server feature-mismatch case reported on Linux with Codex CLI 0.161.0 (see #52085), starting plain `codex` showed:

```text
Background server has incompatible feature settings
This session requires api_key_model_discovery to be enabled

Restart will use these shared feature settings:
  api_key_model_discovery = true
  auth_elicitation = true
  code_mode_host = true
  mcp_oauth_refresh_coordination = false
```

The **Restart with these settings** choice was disabled with `This server is not managed by Codex.`, leaving **Run without daemon this time** and **Cancel**.

The user had not manually started an external app-server and was using Codex clients. The precise process launch path/ownership on that host was not independently captured, so this report does **not** assert an incorrect ownership classification.

A non-disruptive recovery **was** confirmed: `codex --disable api_key_model_discovery` (or persisting `[features] api_key_model_discovery = false` in `~/.codex/config.toml`) allowed plain `codex` to attach to the *existing* server, with ChatGPT authentication, without restarting the server or interrupting other work. That option was not disclosed in the TUI.

## Code path

The wording is directly traceable to:

1. [`app-server-daemon/src/lib.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/47b80571f0d6587060a580c47f6af0cfaefb0d5c/codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/lib.rs#L409-L427): an app-server can answer the socket probe while `running_backend(&settings)` returns `None`.
2. [`tui/src/startup_orchestration.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/47b80571f0d6587060a580c47f6af0cfaefb0d5c/codex-rs/tui/src/startup_orchestration.rs#L542-L573): `managed_daemon = output.backend.is_some()`.
3. [`tui/src/daemon_recovery.rs`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/47b80571f0d6587060a580c47f6af0cfaefb0d5c/codex-rs/tui/src/daemon_recovery.rs#L159-L170): the disabled restart choice translates `!managed_daemon` to `"This server is not managed by Codex."`.

As a result, the UI turns a narrowly defined daemon-management check into a broad statement about “Codex” without disclosing the actual failed criterion.

## Expected behavior

- Use precise terminology, for example: **“The app-server is reachable, but the Codex app-server daemon manager does not recognize it as a managed instance. Automatic restart is unavailable.”**
- Distinguish **server reachability**, **daemon-managed lifecycle ownership**, and **who originally launched the server**. Do not imply a proven launch origin where none was established.
- When the incompatibility is an optional feature flag, show a non-disruptive client-side alternative where applicable (for this case, `codex --disable api_key_model_discovery`), including that it keeps using the existing shared server. Do not present `--no-daemon` as the only non-restart option.
- If useful, point to a read-only daemon-status check and the specific missing management evidence. Continue to refuse potentially disruptive restarts of unowned processes.

## Related, but separate

- #52085 / #51891: feature-default mismatch involving `api_key_model_discovery`.
- #49612: Desktop SSH process/lifecycle ambiguity and unclear recovery.
- #37893: a reachable app-server becoming unmanaged after daemon state loss.
- #24542: Codex Desktop remote proxy starting an app-server outside the managed-daemon lifecycle.

These concern feature compatibility or process lifecycle. This report is specifically about the **misleading TUI diagnosis and absent safe recovery guidance**, which also applies when unmanaged process status is intentional.

items.title: Count interrupted goal continuations toward the no-activity limit
items.body:
Count interrupted goal continuations toward the no-activity limit

## Why

Interrupted automatic goal continuations reset the empty-response counter, allowing repeated interruptions without activity to keep a goal running indefinitely.

## What changed

Count interrupted automatic continuations without activity toward the existing three-turn limit that marks a goal as `blocked`. Defer evaluation until the thread is idle and serialize it with turn-start accounting. Activity and user turns still reset the counter.

## Testing

Extend accounting tests to cover interrupted and mixed empty continuations, including resets after tool activity or user turns. Add an app-server regression case where a `PreCompact` hook repeatedly interrupts automatic continuations and verify the `thread/goal/updated` notification reports `blocked`.

Python strict path resolution fails inside Codex’s Windows command environment for an existing workspace file.

Recorded error:
PermissionError: [WinError 5] Access is denied

Failing call:
pathlib.Path.resolve(strict=True) -> ntpath.realpath

Ordinary file reads, stat operations and SHA256 hashing succeeded. I ran the same strict-resolution check using the same Python interpreter outside Codex in normal Windows PowerShell, where it returned the resolved path successfully.

Additional recorded diagnostics found that QueryDosDeviceW("C:") failed with Windows error 5, while ordinary file access succeeded.

This prevents an integrity verifier from running successfully. The verifier’s strict path checks have not been weakened or bypassed.

Observations were recorded on October 8, 2026.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Open the affected workspace in Codex on Windows.
2. Select an existing file within that workspace.
3. Ask Codex to execute the following read-only command, replacing both placeholders with the actual Python executable and existing file paths:

& '<PYTHON_EXE>' -B -c "from pathlib import Path; print(Path(r'<EXISTING_FILE_ABSOLUTE_PATH>').resolve(strict=True))"

The failure was observed on a specific existing workspace JSON file. Reproducibility on arbitrary files or other machines has not been established.

### What is the expected behavior?

Strict resolution of an existing workspace file that Codex has permission to read should return its resolved absolute path successfully.

If sandbox setup or permissions prevent this, Codex should provide an actionable explanation and a supported recovery procedure without requiring sandbox disablement, broad ACL changes or removal of strict verification.

Platform: Windows NT 10.0.26200.0, x64

The integrity verifier’s strict path checks remain unchanged; no fallback or bypass has been applied. Reproducibility on arbitrary files or other machines has not been established.

Please advise how to confirm the active sandbox backend and recover through a supported procedure.

## Environment
- Codex desktop for Windows, installed package version 26.1002.7124.0.
- Private skills-only plugins imported from GPTs and edited through Plugin Creator.
- Reported on 9 October 2026.

## Problem
Updating plugin logo assets and manifest references successfully creates a new release and updates the locally installed package, but Customize > Plugins continues to show generated fallback icons in the installed sidebar, plugin detail header, and prompt cards. Reproduced with two separate private plugins: one shows a blue folder, the other a blue symbol.

## Reproduction
1. Open an existing private skills-only plugin through Plugin Creator.
2. Replace its icon with a valid 500 x 500 PNG.
3. Set logo and composerIcon in extensions.com.openai.interface in plugin.json and synchronize the existing .codex-plugin/plugin.json overlay.
4. Publish with update_plugin using the observed expected_release_id.
5. Open Customize > Plugins and select the updated plugin.

## Expected
The supplied image appears as the plugin logo and composer icon.

## Actual
The installed version updates, but the fallback icon remains. Reopening the picker and subsequent releases did not resolve it, according to the user.

## Verified findings
- Plugin Creator update calls succeeded and read-back confirmed the new versions, manifest image references, and uploaded assets.
- The locally installed PNG hash matches the supplied source image.
- A later attempt changed the image filename to a fresh path and added logoDark; this did not resolve the displayed icon.
- Adding the skill-level icon_small and icon_large fields did not fix the plugin-level display either.
- Inspection of the installed desktop JavaScript shows plugin icon resolution prefers interface logo/logoUrl and composerIcon/composerIconUrl, then generates an ID-based fallback when no usable logo is provided. The fallback generated for the affected photo plugin ID corresponds to the observed folder icon.

## Investigation request
Please check whether Plugin Creator updates propagate packaged logo assets into remote plugin presentation metadata and whether Customize uses stale remote metadata despite installing the latest release. This is a suspected cause, not a confirmed backend diagnosis.

Private plugin IDs, filesystem paths, brand images, and screenshots are intentionally omitted from this public report.

## Summary

Tasks repeatedly produce assistant messages saying that they have no Project association. In an October 9, 2026 observation, an assistant reported that a task was active in the intended Local working folder while its native Project association remained unconfirmed, citing `projectId: null`.

A subsequent read-only Local inspection found non-null saved native Local Project assignments for both the originally reported task and a diagnostic task created with explicit selection of an existing Project. Neither was explicitly marked projectless in the inspected saved app state.

The issue is the discrepancy between the association warnings and the saved assignments. The earlier null readback was not reproduced, and canonical durable-host membership and current sidebar presentation remain independently unverified. This report does not claim that saved membership was actually lost.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0.1
- Desktop app 26.1007.21159, build 20052
- Bundled CLI protocol 0.162.0
- Observed October 9, 2026
- Local tasks with saved native Project assignments

These are the diagnostic environment values for this follow-up, not measurements of every earlier occurrence.

## Observed sequence and evidence

1. The owner encountered repeated assistant messages reporting absent Project association.
2. One current conversation reported correct Local-folder execution but unconfirmed native association, citing `projectId: null`. This is verified conversation evidence of the assistant's report, not independently captured proof of that earlier native response.
3. A Local diagnostic task was created with explicit Project selection.
4. Read-only saved app-state inspection found non-null native Local Project assignments for both tasks and no explicit projectless marking.
5. Canonical durable-host membership and current UI/sidebar grouping could not be independently verified. No controlled reproduction of the original null response was obtained.

The inspected protocol supports `Thread.projectId` and explicit Project selection for durable-task creation. This establishes available controls, not which creation inputs were used for the earlier task or whether all membership interfaces agree.

## Expected behavior

Keep these four facts distinct and consistently observable:

1. Actual working directory and execution computer.
2. Saved native Project membership.
3. Membership returned by task-list/read interfaces.
4. Visible sidebar grouping.

Assistants should label unresolved association as unverified. A matching working directory alone does not establish membership, and a null field alone does not establish that a saved assignment is absent.

Please investigate incomplete readback, host-specific membership resolution, synchronization and assistant interpretation separately. Any required recovery should preserve existing task IDs and history.

- #51477 and #48728 document related null-membership readbacks despite saved assignments. A shared cause has not been established.

labels.name: bug

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using?

ChatGPT desktop on macOS, **26.1007.21159 (build 20052)**, production channel; bundle identifier `com.openai.codex`. Codex Framework/Chromium: `155.0.8059.40`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.6.1 (25G76), Apple Silicon, **128 GiB physical RAM**.

`uname -mprs`: `Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm`

### What issue are you seeing?

The macOS desktop app repeatedly crashes during use, at irregular intervals. **Four main-process crashes on 2026-10-09 are confirmed V8 JavaScript heap OOMs.** Restarting the Mac did not fix the problem.

At initial reporting, these crashes had not been observed on the preceding version, **26.930.31730 (build 12947)**. **Update, 2026-10-11:** a subsequent rollback also produced two confirmed native JavaScript-heap OOMs on build 12947. The evidence no longer supports treating that version as an unaffected baseline; see the [rollback results and historical code comparison](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/52631#issuecomment-6107808550). No app patch, history reset, or heap-limit override was used for this investigation.

All four native reports identify `CrBrowserMain`, `EXC_BREAKPOINT/SIGTRAP`, and the same framework-relative PC `0x475d754`. Examination of the installed ARM64 framework and saved registers confirms:

- The faulting instruction is `BRK #0` in the V8 OOM callback.
- `x20 - framework_base = 0xe0cb600` resolves to `Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory`.
- `x24 = 1` selects the JavaScript-heap OOM branch. The caller references `CALL_AND_RETRY_LAST`.
- Framework SHA-256: `156ac7655cf758be69a3a441aeb3ef488a4d8b77c30b2a3f3fed6c26f7e6bc8b`.

Each crash closely followed oversized `thread-stream-state-changed` warnings. Times below are CEST (UTC+02:00):

| Crash time | Oversized warnings in process | Payload size | Last warning to crash |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| 08:57:14.327 | 72 | 424.8–458.7 MB | 1.331 s |
| 09:13:53.381 | 37 | 437.0–451.5 MB | 1.354 s |
| 10:10:01.869 | 110 | 437.8–524.2 MB | 1.114 s |
| 18:23:39.282, after reboot | 17 | Final payload: 460,739,840 bytes | 2.204 s |

Representative sanitized log line preceding the fourth crash:

```text
2026-10-09T16:23:37.078Z warning [IpcClient] [IPC] Dropping broadcast: payload too large maxIpcFrameBytes=268435456 method=thread-stream-state-changed payloadBytes=460739840
```

In the installed `app.asar/.vite/build/src-BJv5Mk7n.js`, `sendBroadcast` performs `JSON.stringify` and `Buffer.byteLength` **before** rejecting payloads above 256 MiB. Oversized messages are dropped before socket transmission, but after the serialization allocation. The snapshot path includes the full enumerable `conversationState`.

This is evidence of a likely contributing allocation path, not proof of the exact failed allocation, responsible thread/field, or a memory leak. The warnings do not distinguish snapshots from patch messages.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

No deterministic minimal reproduction is available yet.

1. Launch the current macOS desktop app and use local Codex chats.
2. Continue normal chat/tool work. The app intermittently terminates; this is not limited to initial launch.
3. Reopen the app. Failures recur, including after a full Mac reboot.

A specific chat or action has not been isolated. No private conversation transcript or full application log is attached.

### What is the expected behavior?

The desktop app remains usable without repeated termination. Conversation-state handling should stay within bounded memory usage, including before serialization and when rejecting oversized messages.

### Additional information

Separate renderer crashes were also recorded after reboot, followed by UI reconstruction while the main process remained alive. Their native cause is not established and should not be assumed to be the same OOM. The four main-process crashes above are independently confirmed.

Related desktop reports, not confirmed duplicates:

- #52622: same version/build, but **startup** failure with `Zone Allocation failed - process out of memory`; this report concerns **runtime JavaScript heap OOM** with oversized-state evidence.
- #44256: earlier desktop version, deterministic crash when opening a specific long thread.
- #52532: same version, renderer freeze/high CPU rather than the confirmed main-process heap OOM reported here.

Please investigate the possible version regression and conversation-state allocation path, and advise whether a supported temporary workaround is available.

items.body:
## Summary

The Codex integration inside IntelliJ shows a stale model list and tries to use models that are no longer supported for a ChatGPT-authenticated Codex account.

The standalone Codex CLI on the same machine/account works correctly and exposes the current model catalog, including GPT-6.1 Sol.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10 x64
- IntelliJ IDEA: 2026.1.3
- JetBrains AI Assistant plugin: 261.25134.239
- Standalone Codex CLI: 0.162.0
- Authentication: ChatGPT account
- Plan: ChatGPT Plus

## Actual behavior in IntelliJ

The Codex model picker in IntelliJ only shows:

- GPT-5.4
- GPT-5.4-Mini
- GPT-5.3-Codex
- GPT-5.2

Selecting GPT-5.4 fails with:

```
The 'gpt-5.4' model is not supported when using Codex with a ChatGPT account.
```

Updating the standalone Codex installation and the JetBrains AI Assistant plugin, then restarting IntelliJ, does not refresh the picker.

## Standalone CLI behavior

On the same machine and ChatGPT account:

```
codex --version
codex-cli 0.162.0
```

Inside the CLI, `/status` shows:

- model: GPT-6.1-Sol
- account: Plus
- weekly usage remaining: 100%

The local Codex model cache is also current:

- `client_version: 0.162.0`
- contains `gpt-6.1-sol`
- contains GPT-6 Astra / GPT-6 Sol / GPT-6 Luna
- contains GPT-5.6 Sol / Terra / Luna

So this does not appear to be an account limit, stale standalone CLI, or stale local Codex model cache problem.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install/update standalone Codex on Windows to 0.162.0.
2. Authenticate with a ChatGPT account.
3. Verify in CLI that GPT-6.1-Sol is available and works.
4. Use IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1.3 with JetBrains AI Assistant 261.25134.239.
5. Open the Codex panel/model picker.
6. Observe that the picker still exposes only GPT-5.4 / GPT-5.4-Mini / GPT-5.3-Codex / GPT-5.2.
7. Select GPT-5.4.
8. Observe the unsupported-model error for ChatGPT authentication.

## Expected behavior

The IntelliJ Codex integration should use a model catalog compatible with the authenticated Codex account and should expose the same currently supported models as the Codex runtime, or at minimum avoid offering models that the backend immediately rejects.

## Notes

This makes the IDE integration effectively unusable even though the standalone CLI works correctly. It looks like the JetBrains integration/model picker is using a stale or separate model catalog/runtime from the updated standalone Codex installation.

Publishing an already saved and successfully built site version repeatedly failed with “Failed to publish the built site”. An earlier attempt also reported “Unable to authenticate request”.

Complete a build and save a new site version.

Continue working on the project; cloud command execution fails with an executor transport disconnection and a 25-second recovery timeout.

Retry from an incognito browser session.

Request a small source-code change in the same conversation: execution and file-editing capabilities remain unavailable.

Repeated retries have not restored the development environment.

A deployment failure should leave the development environment usable.

VS Code ### What platform is your computer? macOS ### What issue are you seeing? I started a new Codex conversation and submitted a task to correct terminology in four Gateman client READMEs. The correct prompt was stored at: 3f8442be-4224-4958-bc0f-750e0b06d5f0/Pasted text.txt Codex initially acknowledged the correct terminology task. However, its first shell command attempted to read the attachment using an incorrect path with an additional d appended to the attachment UUID. The shell command suppressed the resulting file-read error and used an || fallback to read another attachment: ea58abc0-9607-40ec-bf5e-9cf926b5ccd5/Pasted text.txt I verified that this second attachment contained an entirely unrelated Square Sandbox verification task from outside the current conversation. Codex then executed that unrelated task, making two live Square Sandbox API requests through my Gateman application. These produced two operation accounting records. No Square-side mutations or source-code modifications were reported. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? ### Steps to reproduce 1. Open the Codex extension in VS Code within an existing project workspace. 2. Start a completely new Codex conversation. 3. Submit several lengthy task prompts that VS Code stores as generated `Pasted text.txt` attachments. 4. Submit another lengthy prompt, in this case titled **"Codex Task — Correct Gateman Client Terminology"**. 5. Verify that the correct prompt was saved under its generated attachment directory. 6. Allow Codex to process the task and inspect its initial file-reading commands. ### Actual behaviour observed Codex correctly acknowledged the terminology task but attempted to read its attachment using an incorrect filesystem path. The correct attachment ID was: `3f8442be-4224-4958-bc0f-750e0b06d5f0` Codex attempted to read: `3f8442be-4224-4958-bc0f-750e0b06d5f0d` Notice the additional `d` at the end. Its shell command suppressed the resulting error using `2>/dev/null` and included an `||` fallback. The fallback accessed another attachment: `ea58abc0-9607-40ec-bf5e-9cf926b5ccd5` That attachment contained an unrelated Square Sandbox API verification task from a different conversation. Codex proceeded to execute the unrelated task, making two live Square Sandbox API requests through the application, rather than performing the requested documentation corrections. ### Expected behaviour Codex should read only the attachment associated with the current user request. If the attachment cannot be read, it should report the error rather than silently substituting another attachment. Instructions obtained from unrelated attachments must not override or replace the current task. ### Reproducibility This incident has been observed once. I have not deliberately attempted to reproduce it because the failure resulted in unintended live API operations. Screenshots of the attachment paths, shell command and execution history are attached. ### What is the expected behavior? Codex should read the exact attachment associated with the current user message. If that attachment cannot be read, it should stop and report the failure. It must not substitute a previous attachment and execute unrelated instructions. Impact This is a task-isolation and execution-boundary failure. The original task required documentation-only changes, yet Codex initiated unrelated live API operations. ### Additional information Evidence available Screenshot of the correct pasted-text attachment. Screenshot showing Codex's initial acknowledgement of the correct task. Screenshot of the shell command containing the incorrect attachment path and fallback. items.title: Profiles that extend ":workspace" lose the read-only protection of .git/.codex/.agents/.aws (docs say it is kept)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: config
labels.description: Issues involving config.toml, config keys, config merging, or config updates

items.body:
### What version of Codex is running?

codex-cli 0.161.0 (macOS, Seatbelt). The source involved is byte-identical in rust-v0.162.0. As of commit 9a59289f (2026-10-09), `main` has the same code.

### What happened?

A permission profile with `extends = ":workspace"` does not keep the built-in read-only protection of `.git` and `.codex` under the workspace root. The built-in `:workspace` profile keeps them read-only. A profile that only extends it makes them writable, so a sandboxed command can write `.git/config` or `.git/hooks/*`. Git then runs that code unsandboxed the next time someone runs a git command outside the sandbox. We reproduced this end to end with a `core.fsmonitor` entry that a later `git status` ran.

The docs say the opposite. The example in https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/permissions.md reads:

```toml
[permissions.workspace-only]
# By extending the :workspace profile, you get Codex's safeguards to ensure
# subfolders such as .codex/ and .git/ within a workspace root are read-only
# while the rest of the folder is writable.
extends = ":workspace"
```

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/repro/home /tmp/repro/ws && cd /tmp/repro/ws && git init -q .
cat > /tmp/repro/home/config.toml <<'TOML'
[permissions.ext]
extends = ":workspace"

[permissions.ext-fixed]
extends = ":workspace"

[permissions.ext-fixed.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
".git" = "read"
".codex" = "read"
TOML
for p in ':workspace' ext ext-fixed; do
  CODEX_HOME=/tmp/repro/home codex sandbox -P "$p" -C /tmp/repro/ws -- /bin/sh -c 'echo x >> .git/config'; a=$?
  CODEX_HOME=/tmp/repro/home codex sandbox -P "$p" -C /tmp/repro/ws -- /bin/sh -c 'mkdir -p .codex/t'; b=$?
  echo "$p git_config=$a dot_codex=$b"
done
```

Observed (1 = denied, 0 = written):

```
:workspace git_config=1 dot_codex=1
ext git_config=0 dot_codex=0
ext-fixed git_config=1 dot_codex=1
```

In our fuller runs `.agents` and `.aws` behave the same way. Listing the names explicitly under `":workspace_roots"`, as in `ext-fixed`, restores the protection. We use that as a workaround.

### Likely cause (code reading, not proven at runtime)

When a profile names `:workspace` in `extends`, `extensible_builtin_parent_profile` in `codex-rs/core/src/config/permissions.rs` builds the parent from `FileSystemSandboxPolicy::workspace_write(...)` and converts it to TOML through `permission_profile_toml_from_file_system_policy`. That conversion calls `insert_filesystem_permission_toml`, which starts with:

```rust
if entry.skips_missing_path() {
    return;
}
```

`workspace_write` adds the `.git` / `.agents` / `.codex` / `.aws` read-only entries as skip-missing entries (`append_default_read_only_project_root_subpath_if_no_explicit_rule` in `codex-rs/protocol/src/permissions.rs`). So they look like they are dropped from the parent that the child profile inherits.

### What is the expected behavior?

A profile that extends `:workspace` keeps the same protected subpaths as the built-in `:workspace` profile, as the docs say. Failing that, the docs should state that the protection is not inherited and show the explicit entries.

### Related

- #37081 (nested repository `.git` not covered)
- #49303 (linked worktree common git dir)
- #50098 (`.aws` missing from the documented protected-paths list)

## Problem

## Environment

- Local bundled CLI: 0.162.0-alpha.2
- macOS 27.0.1, Apple Silicon
- Desktop has local sessions and an SSH-connected Mac Studio
- Observed October 9, 2026

## Affected thread IDs

These three IDs appear in desktop log entries containing resume failures and the missing-rollout error:

- `01a096b1-1132-7f41-8dbb-17eaad0c5c7f`
- `01a09694-1f08-78f0-8d97-c2b6fba136ac`
- `01a09416-dbc7-7160-8f68-ca2361ec7043`

An additional conversation ID, `6ac606d7-1308-83ee-b062-d752a4154180`, has the same missing-rollout error during `thread/queue/list`, but no matching resume failure was found. It is listed separately because it may be a different routing issue.

## Reproduction on the affected account

1. Open one of the affected existing chats in the desktop app.
2. Observe the failed resume / missing-rollout error.
3. Attempt to delete the broken task.
4. Observe the deletion failure. Deletion was specifically investigated for `01a096b1-1132-7f41-8dbb-17eaad0c5c7f`; we have not verified deletion failures individually for the other two IDs.

## Observed diagnostics

For `01a096b1-1132-7f41-8dbb-17eaad0c5c7f`:

- Desktop route referenced the SSH-connected host.
- At 2026-10-09T15:27:52Z, `thread/delete` returned code `-32600`: `no rollout found for thread id 01a096b1-1132-7f41-8dbb-17eaad0c5c7f`.

- Deletion through the SSH host's app-server using `codex delete --remote unix:// --force <id>` also failed.
- Read-only inspection found no row for this specific ID in either machine's default `state_5.sqlite` threads table.
- Local `codex doctor` reported healthy database integrity and matching local rollout/database inventory.

The cause is not established. The missing rollout and placement-format errors may reflect different routing/fallback attempts rather than the same failure.

An existing task should resume from its correct storage location. If its transcript is unavailable, permanent deletion should still provide a supported way to remove the stale task entry, or clearly explain how to recover/remove it.

I have attributed the growth to Codex because the same folder names begin appearing again after I restart Codex, and new temporary items continue to appear while I work. 4. Continue using Codex for a few days and observe the item count reach the millions.
5. Close and restart Codex; the same folder names begin appearing again, with further temporary items created during use.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should clean up temporary files and folders when they are no longer needed, or otherwise keep its Temp usage bounded. Ordinary use over a few days should not leave millions of accumulated items requiring tens of minutes of manual deletion.

### Additional information

- Platform: Windows (exact Windows version not yet recorded).

No security setting, permission, authentication, or sandbox configuration was changed, and no existing session was resumed or interrupted.

### Related reports
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/52482
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48759
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/44309

This report adds the user's full-access-versus-sandbox comparison and the exact exec-server -32603 failure. The underlying Windows setup/policy cause remains unverified.
